## My Reasoning

I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over 30 years. I know what works here and what doesn't. The wheat-maize rotation is what everyone in my village does, and it's what this flat, irrigated land is suited for. I'm not going to experiment with something new at my age — I need reliable income and I know these two crops.

My family has about 7 mu of contracted land. It's all on the flat plain, good loam soil. After my husband's health got worse, I handle most of the fieldwork myself, though I hire a tractor service for tillage and sometimes a neighbor's son to help with harvest.

**Wheat** goes in this October. I'll buy the improved variety — Jimai 22 or whatever the seed store in town is selling that did well for my neighbor last year. I won't buy hybrid wheat seeds; those aren't really a thing here and would cost too much anyway. I'll apply compound fertilizer as a base before planting and add urea at jointing. I need to irrigate at least 3 times — once before winter sets in, once at jointing, once when the grain is filling. Our groundwater is deep now but the pump still works. I'll spray for weeds in spring and do one fungicide spray for powdery mildew. Rotary tillage before planting to break up the maize stubble.

**Maize** goes in right after wheat harvest in June, no-till, directly into the stubble. No need to hire a tractor for that. I'll use hybrid seed — everyone uses hybrid maize now, the yield difference is real. One urea top-dressing when the plants are knee-high. Summer rains are usually enough, but I'll irrigate once if we get a dry August like last year. Spray herbicide once, and maybe once more for borer if I see the damage early.

I won't risk trying cotton or vegetables on the main fields. My back isn't what it was and I can't manage the extra labor. The grain market is stable and I know the costs.
